items.label: Fireball — Tap
items.query: What does tap Fireball do, what target situation is it best for, and how does it differ from charging Fireball?
items.candidate_text: A quick, mobile shot against a single or separated enemy. Unlike charging, it costs less mana and doesn't restrict your movement—useful for picking off isolated threats rather than damaging clustered groups.

chunks.title: Player actions: movement and Fireball
chunks.text:
Action: Move and Aim. What the player does: Use WASD to move and the mouse to aim. Purpose: Circle crowds and protect escape routes.

Action: Fireball. What the player does: Tap for a quick, mobile shot against a single or separated enemy. Hold to charge: costs more mana and restricts movement further, rewarding preparation by damaging multiple clustered enemies. Purpose: Rewards distance and preparation; a charge's area advantage matters against groups, not against one target.

chunks.title: Charged Fireball interactions
chunks.text: Spell: Charged Fireball. Against Melee Enemies: Melee enemies naturally cluster while pursuing the wizard, making them strong area-damage targets. Charging becomes unsafe once they close the distance. Against Ranged Enemies: Telegraphed ranged attacks force the player to keep moving, reducing the time available for a full charge. Quick shots are safer but provide less damage and area.

chunks.title: Peer and agent review revision
chunks.text: Peer feedback identified that the earlier draft did not explain how the spells and room layouts produced different tactical decisions. A targeted multi-agent review then tested whether those decisions could collapse into a dominant strategy. This revision clarifies Fireball's tap-versus-charge tradeoff, Frost Field's resource commitment, Force Wave's mid-room-versus-door decision, mixed enemy compositions, persistent-pursuer priority, and room-specific implementation checks without adding mechanics or expanding the required scope.

chunks.title: Target player experience
chunks.text: The player should feel powerful for a few seconds and vulnerable immediately afterward: control a corridor, charge a Fireball, sprint to a door, and lock it just before the crowd arrives. Pounding from the other side makes the next decision urgent.

critic.summary: Mostly faithful, but the claim that tap Fireball "doesn't restrict your movement" turns a comparative statement in the evidence into an absolute one.

issues.problematic_claim: it costs less mana and doesn't restrict your movement
issues.explanation: The evidence only states that charging 'costs more mana and restricts movement further' — the word 'further' is comparative and implies tap already carries some baseline movement constraint, with charging adding more on top. The generated text converts this into an absolute claim that tap has zero movement restriction, which is not directly supported by the retrieved evidence.
issues.revision_instruction: Rephrase to a comparative framing (e.g., 'restricts movement less than charging') rather than asserting tap has no movement restriction at all.

items.label: Fireball — Charged
items.query: What does Charged Fireball do, when is charging useful, and what makes charging unsafe against melee and ranged pressure?
items.candidate_text: Charge it to punish enemies who've clustered while chasing you. Melee foes that close the distance make charging risky. Ranged attacks force you to keep moving, cutting your window short—a quick cast is safer but weaker.

chunks.title: Charged Fireball interactions
chunks.text: Spell: Charged Fireball. Against Melee Enemies: Melee enemies naturally cluster while pursuing the wizard, making them strong area-damage targets. Charging becomes unsafe once they close the distance. Against Ranged Enemies: Telegraphed ranged attacks force the player to keep moving, reducing the time available for a full charge. Quick shots are safer but provide less damage and area.

chunks.title: Force Wave interactions and distinct spell roles
chunks.text:
Spell: Force Wave. Against Melee Enemies: The primary emergency response when melee enemies surround the wizard or block access to a door. Its long cooldown prevents repeated use. Against Ranged Enemies: Its short range makes it a poor answer to distant ranged pressure. Reaching a ranged enemy to use it may expose the wizard to the melee group.

The three spells solve different problems: Frost Field controls pursuit, Force Wave repairs an immediate positioning mistake, and Charged Fireball converts a previously created opening into damage. No single spell reliably answers both enemy types by itself. Force Wave's cooldown is tuned so an encounter space typically allows only about one meaningful use: spending it to escape a mid-room surround may leave none available for that room's door attempt, and saving it for the door means resolving mid-room danger without it. This is an intentional resource decision, not proof that either use was wrong.

chunks.title: Game facts and conditions
chunks.text:
Genre: Top-down dark-fantasy survival action. Platform: Windows PC.

Playable Content: One handcrafted floor; five connected spaces. Player Character: One vulnerable wizard; no class selection.

Core Abilities: Charged Fireball, Frost Field, Force Wave. Core Enemies: Melee Enemy and Ranged Enemy.

Win Condition: Open the final door and escape. Loss Condition: The wizard reaches zero health.

chunks.title: Executive summary: core survival loop
chunks.text:
No Safe Circle is a single-player, top-down survival action game set on one handcrafted dungeon floor. The player controls a vulnerable wizard who can destroy small groups of monsters with powerful spells but cannot survive being surrounded. The player must control distance, wait for mana to regenerate, and decide when to fight, flee, or risk opening the next sealed door.

Each room ends at a door that takes five uninterrupted seconds to open. Before attempting it, the player must create space by luring enemies away, slowing them with Frost Field, knocking them back with Force Wave, or defeating enough of them to reduce the immediate threat. Enemies can follow the wizard through an open doorway. After crossing, the player can close and lock the door, but surviving pursuers will pound against it and eventually break through.

Locked doors provide recovery time, not permanent safety. In the final room, the player must create enough distance from the pursuing enemies to open the final door and escape. The player wins by passing through the final door and loses if the wizard's health reaches zero.

critic.summary: Generated text accurately reflects nsc-gdd-009: clustering melee targets, risk once melee close the distance, ranged attacks forcing movement, and the quick-cast tradeoff. No values were invented and no absolutes were introduced.

items.label: Frost Field
items.query: What are Frost Field's interactions and limitations against melee and ranged enemies?
items.candidate_text: A field of icy ground heavily slows anything caught inside. Strongest against melee groups—it stretches their formation and buys space to act. Ranged enemies are slowed too, but can still fire, so keep moving to avoid their shots.

chunks.title: Frost Field interactions and limitations
chunks.text: Spell: Frost Field. Against Melee Enemies: Strongest against melee groups because it slows direct pursuit, stretches the formation, and creates an opening to charge Fireball or begin opening a door — though it draws a meaningful share of the shared mana pool and does not guarantee a fully safe charge in every position or against every group. Against a small or loosely spaced group, direct positioning, a partial charge, or tap Fireball can be the better resource decision. Against Ranged Enemies: Slows a ranged enemy's repositioning but does not stop its attacks. The player must still move laterally or use room geometry to avoid incoming shots.

chunks.title: Room 5: Final Room
chunks.text: Area: 5. Final Room. Layout and Tactical Purpose: A comparatively open chamber with limited cover and one central obstacle, populated by both Melee and Ranged Enemies. The player must combine movement, Frost Field, Force Wave, and Fireball to create the final uninterrupted five-second escape window.

chunks.text: Spell: Charged Fireball. Against Melee Enemies: Melee enemies naturally cluster while pursuing the wizard, making them strong area-damage targets. critic.summary: Frost Field text overstates its area of effect and drops the mana-cost/no-guarantee caveat that makes its melee use a real tradeoff rather than a free win.

issues.explanation: The evidence only supports Frost Field slowing melee pursuit and ranged enemy repositioning. 'Anything caught inside' generalizes the effect beyond enemies (implying the player or other entities are also affected) without support, mirroring the flagged pattern of describing a slow effect as applying to 'anything' unless the player is also a supported target.
issues.revision_instruction: Scope the slow to enemies specifically (e.g., 'heavily slows enemies caught inside') rather than 'anything caught inside.'

issues.problematic_claim: Strongest against melee groups—it stretches their formation and buys space to act.
issues.explanation: The evidence qualifies this benefit: it draws a meaningful share of the shared mana pool, does not guarantee a fully safe charge in every position or against every group, and against a small or loosely spaced group a different action (direct positioning, partial charge, tap Fireball) can be the better resource decision. The generated line presents the melee benefit as an unqualified positive, removing the intentional resource tradeoff.
issues.revision_instruction: Add a brief qualifier noting the mana cost and that it doesn't guarantee a safe charge against every group, so the tradeoff isn't lost.

items.label: Force Wave
items.query: When should the player use Force Wave, what does it do, and why can it not be used repeatedly?
items.candidate_text: A short-range radial knockback that shoves nearby enemies back, clearing space when you're surrounded or blocked from a door. Its long cooldown means only one meaningful use per encounter—save it for a true emergency.

chunks.title: Core gameplay loop
chunks.text:
The player moves through connected rooms toward the final door. In each room, the objective is to create five safe seconds, open the next door, cross through it, and lock it before the pursuing monsters arrive.

1. Scout the room, locate the sealed door, and identify a route for luring or slowing enemies.

2. Avoid the group, pull part of it away, or spend mana on a direct fight.

3. Use Frost Field and movement to stretch the chase; charge Fireball when enough distance exists.

4. Use Force Wave if enemies reach the wizard or block the door.

5. Open the door for five uninterrupted seconds, cross through it, lock it, and recover before pursuers break through.

chunks.title: Player experience success criteria
chunks.text:
A first-time player understands that reaching a door is not enough; five safe seconds are required.

The player understands that enemies left alive remain a threat: leaving them alive means locking a door while they attack it, and later encountering them if that door breaks through.

Encounters use three to eight enemies and never exceed fifteen active enemies.

Failure is readable: poor positioning, low mana, using Force Wave without an immediate threat and leaving it unavailable when critical space is needed, or waiting too long.

chunks.title: Player actions: Frost Field and Force Wave
chunks.text:
Action: Frost Field. What the player does: Place a temporary area that heavily slows enemies. Purpose: Divides crowds and protects routes.

Action: Force Wave. What the player does: Use a short-range radial knockback with a long cooldown. Purpose: Creates emergency space.

critic.summary: Text is mostly faithful (correct knockback description, emergency-space purpose, no invented damage/stun) but the cooldown claim drops the GDD's explicit qualifiers, turning a typical/approximate limit into an absolute rule.

issues.problematic_claim: Its long cooldown means only one meaningful use per encounter
issues.explanation: The evidence states the cooldown 'is tuned so an encounter space typically allows only about one meaningful use' and explicitly frames the choice between an early mid-room use and saving it for the door as 'an intentional resource decision, not proof that either use was wrong.' The generated line drops 'typically' and 'about,' converting an approximate, context-dependent limit into an absolute per-encounter cap, which overstates the certainty of the rule.
issues.revision_instruction: Reinsert a qualifier (e.g., 'typically only about one meaningful use') so the cooldown limit reads as approximate rather than an absolute per-encounter cap.
